title: Planning his solos mentally before touching the horn
summary: He denies only two solos were planned and describes mentally rehearsing theme, variations and band entries before playing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: In Barry Ulanov's book on Duke Ellington, there is a statement that says on the "Shiek of Arabia", Lawrence plays what he says was one of the only two solos that he ever planned through from beginning to end. The other one was "Rose of the Rio Grande". Is that true?

Partially. Partially. The only thing is that whenever I would be given a solo, you know, where the whole number sort of depended on me, I would plan the whole number. I had a system which I used to try to perfect these solos. I wouldn't get up and just play anything that

came across my mind. I would first go into a study without the horn. I would mentally play the lead -- I mean the theme, then with slight deviations, and then with more deviations, and then hear where the band would come in and make embellishments, and then I would come in with more.
And when I got through with this routine, I could hear myself play the number as I wanted to hear it, and still not have touched the horn. Then after that, I'd pick up the horn and play it.
So that you did that everytime, not just on the two that -- the two instances.

No. No. No. I did that almost every time. You see, in that band also, when you were given a solo that nobody -- that's your composition, your composition for that particular -- the way you wanted to hear it played. I mean you routine it the way you want it. Nobody framed it for you. Said play this, play that. No, you did that yourself. And it usually worked so that it would sound the best to yourself, see.

At a recording session, you'd have to do that pretty rapidly, wouldn't you, because the recording session that -- some that you've mentioned and some I've been at, Duke would sometimes pass out the music, and then you'd play it.
Well, most of the time the music at

recording session had been played several times at dances and theaters and things before. Then you finally thought it was good enough to record. Then you'd go in and record it. After you've played it a number of times, you pretty well had what you wanted to play set in your mind. So, therefore, it didn't take too long to work it out.
